supplement.where: PDF pp. 16-29, Supplementary Information; availability stated on p. 11.
supplement.holds: Recruitment, human condition allocations and random assignment (p. 16); game procedure and questionnaires (pp. 16-17); contribution definitions, agent prompts and annotation procedure (pp. 17-20); influence-network method (pp. 20-21); Supplementary Figures 1-8 (pp. 22-28); and Supplementary Table 1 (p. 29). Figures 5-6 provide printed lexical/conceptual contribution labels under trait and model manipulations without uncertainty estimates. Figure 8a's individually labeled human nodes establish a figure-derived lower bound of 55 analyzed humans in Study A. No separate exact consensus-analysis human totals or corresponding standard errors are supplied. Table 1 supplies HC3 standard errors for self-reported adoption willingness, not output consensus/diversity.

paper_design_summary: University-recruited volunteers were randomly assigned to conditions in three web-based tangram-description studies, varying AI co-player proportion, behavioral prompts or model size (PDF p. 16). Over repeated rounds, humans wrote descriptions and received partner descriptions and similarity feedback; output measures assess mixed-group consensus, linguistic content and agent influence (pp. 7-9, 16). Study A's influence networks establish at least 55 analyzed humans by counting labeled human nodes, while exact consensus-specific counts and the observation unit of its tests remain unreported (pp. 20-21, 28).

ai_tool.how_used: LLM agents participate as anonymous co-players, generating their own descriptions and adapting through repeated interaction. Human players can use descriptions received in preceding rounds; they cannot see the current partner's description before submission and are instructed not to use external language models. This is exposure to generative-AI peer contributions, not open chatbot access. PDF pp. 4, 16 and 18-19.

task.description: Collaborative referential-description/convention-formation game: repeatedly write one English sentence describing the same ambiguous tangram, then receive the randomly paired partner’s sentence and a similarity payoff. The task has no prescribed vocabulary or correct answer and rewards convergence. It is coded other as a referential communication task; the codebook includes writing tasks compared across people for similarity regardless of this task-type label (PDF pp. 2, 16, 18).
task.duration: 40 rounds; recommended response time 60 seconds per round. Total elapsed session duration is not stated (PDF p. 16, Game Procedure).

outcomes.name: Final consensus strength (diversity sign reversed)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Final-round semantic similarity of the mixed human-agent descriptions. Methods M1 computes each player’s mean cosine similarity to all other players, centers it by that player’s across-round mean, restores the run grand mean, and aggregates to the group endpoint C(T). This identifies a player-level constituent and a set-level endpoint but does not identify the observations used for the reported z tests or boxplots. Neither participant nor set can be confirmed as the unit of the paper’s statistical analysis, so unit is null (PDF p. 7, M1, equations 1-2; pp. 2, 4, 12, 14).

diversity_detail.metric: Consensus strength C(T): average pairwise cosine similarity after the paper's within-player centering and group aggregation; larger values indicate greater similarity.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: all-MiniLM-L6-v2; mean pooling and L2 normalization (PDF p. 7, Methods M1).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each final-round description against all other descriptions in the same session, followed by aggregation over the session. N = 24 counts human and agent players together, not 24 human participants in AI conditions (PDF pp. 7 and 16).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: The paper reports z statistics and p values without identifying the observations, exact test, resampling scheme or dependence correction. Figure 1b’s caption states 95% CI, although its panel displays boxplots; numerical CI limits and their construction are not stated. Figure 3d/f also displays boxplots without defining their observation unit. Independent-session replication and participant- or session-clustered precision are not established (PDF pp. 2, 4, 7, 12, 14).
diversity_detail.notes: Contrast directions reverse similarity to the codebook’s diversity convention. Statistics keep their printed signs. The score pools human and AI descriptions and does not isolate diversity across human writers. No effect size, unprinted mean, standard error, number of independent sessions or analyzed-human count has been derived.

outcomes.name: Lexical-level agent contribution to final consensus (Clex)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Computed from the mixed human-agent output pool. Attribution measures whose expressions enter the consensus, not the number or diversity of ideas and not rated creativity. No uncertainty estimates are printed. Words appearing in each of the last five rounds define the stable consensus vocabulary after lowercasing, stop-word removal and lemmatization. Agent/human usage in the default three-round window from first appearance is normalized by population shares; word scores are averaged using final-five-round usage weights. Early-window variants are grouped here; Supplementary Figure 4 tests windows of 1–3 rounds. Supplementary Figure 2 shows word origins and usage counts. PDF pp. 7, 17, 23 and 25.

outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Computed from the mixed human-agent output pool. Attribution measures whose expressions enter the consensus, not the number or diversity of ideas and not rated creativity. outcomes.name: Measured adoption of a partner's expression
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Methods M4, equation (5), defines adoption(i,r) as sim(e_i^(r), e_partner^(r)) minus sim(e_i^(r-1), e_partner^(r)). This is a change in similarity between different players' produced descriptions, coded diversity/across_people as a dyadic convergence measure; positive adoption indicates increased alignment. It is distinct from movement toward an initial group centroid and from self-reported adoption willingness. The paper compares early rounds 1-20 with late rounds 21-40 across conditions; the aggregation unit, condition weighting and baseline-condition inclusion are not specified. Human-versus-agent contrasts below compare player types and their phase changes, not randomized human treatment arms. AI co-players remain available during the mixed-condition game; the outputs are not after-AI assessments. PDF p. 4, adoption/persistence results; p. 9, Methods M4, equation (5); p. 14, Figure 3b; p. 16, Game Procedure.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Human players, early phase (rounds 1-20; conditions pooled as reported)
contrasts.control_arm: Agent players, early phase (rounds 1-20; conditions pooled as reported)
contrasts.reported: In the early phase, humans adopt substantially more than agents: U = 1735, p < 0.001. Numerical phase means are not printed. Direction reverses adoption similarity to diversity; this is a player-type comparison.

contrasts.reported: Adoption decline, humans versus agents: Δ = -0.055 versus -0.020; U = 671, p < 0.001. Direction reverses the reported change in adoption similarity, not a difference in final diversity levels. This is a comparison of within-game changes by player type, not an AI-versus-control treatment effect.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4, adoption/persistence results, second paragraph; p. 14, Figure 3b.

diversity_detail.metric: Change in cosine similarity of a player's expression to a partner's expression, as printed in equation (5). Larger positive values indicate increased dyadic alignment.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: all-MiniLM-L6-v2; the same model is used for all embedding-based analyses (PDF p. 16, Game Procedure).
diversity_detail.computed_over: The player's current and preceding descriptions relative to the current partner expression; early versus late game phases and human versus agent strata. The analysis includes AI expressions and is not human-only diversity.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: The source prints U statistics and p values, but does not identify the aggregation unit, dependence correction, condition weighting or construction of the Figure 3b error bars (PDF pp. 4, 9 and 14).
diversity_detail.notes: Similarity directions are reversed for diversity coding. Adoption is an alignment-change mechanism, not an absolute final diversity score. Player-type comparisons are labeled other; no randomized human AI effect or standardized effect is inferred.

outcomes.name: Measured persistence of a player's own expression
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity between the same player's descriptions in consecutive rounds, using all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Higher values indicate more stable wording, not higher creativity or diversity across different people. Methods M4 prose refers to rounds r and r+1, whereas equation (6) uses r and r-1; the adjacent-round index convention is not settled. The paper compares early rounds 1-20 and late rounds 21-40 across conditions, without identifying the statistical aggregation unit or condition weighting. The recorded contrast compares human and agent player types' within-game changes, not randomized human treatment arms. AI remains available during mixed-condition play, so this is not after_ai. PDF p. 4, adoption/persistence results; p. 9, Methods M4, equation (6); p. 14, Figure 3c; p. 16, Game Procedure.

contrasts.reported: Persistence increase, humans versus agents: Δ = +0.143 versus +0.059; U = 1702, p < 0.001. Numerical early- and late-phase means are not printed. Direction concerns persistence itself, not creativity.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4, adoption/persistence results, second paragraph; p. 14, Figure 3c.

outcomes.name: Individual influence from reverse PageRank of description-change networks
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: For interacting players, cosine alignment between one player's expression-embedding change and the direction toward the other's previous expression defines directional influence. The stronger nonnegative direction is retained within each round; weights for each ordered pair are averaged across rounds. PageRank on the reversed network assigns one influence score per human or agent player, with damping factor 0.85. The paper's N = 24 is mixed human-and-agent players per network, not 24 humans. This output-derived attribution measure is not a creativity rating or a diversity score. The contrasts compare human and agent strata within conditions, not randomized human treatment arms. Figure 8a's labeled human nodes establish a figure-derived lower bound of 55 analyzed humans in Study A, as documented in participants.exclusions; that bound is not an outcome-specific consensus N. PDF pp. 20-21, Influence Network Analysis, equations S6-S7; p. 28, Supplementary Figure 8.

task.description: Collaborative referential-description/convention-formation game: repeatedly write one English sentence describing the same ambiguous tangram, then receive the randomly paired partner’s sentence and a similarity payoff. The task has no prescribed vocabulary or correct answer and rewards convergence. It is coded other as a referential communication task; the codebook includes writing tasks compared across people for similarity regardless of this task-type label (PDF pp. 2, 16, 18).
task.duration: 40 rounds; recommended response time 60 seconds per round. Total elapsed session duration is not stated (PDF p. 16, Game Procedure).

outcomes.name: Final consensus strength under agent-capability manipulation (diversity sign reversed)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Final-round semantic similarity of the mixed human-agent descriptions. Methods M1 computes each player’s mean cosine similarity to all other players, centers it by that player’s across-round mean, restores the run grand mean, and aggregates to the group endpoint C(T). This identifies a player-level constituent and a set-level endpoint but does not identify the observations used for the reported z tests or boxplots. Neither participant nor set can be confirmed as the unit of the paper’s statistical analysis, so unit is null (PDF p. 7, M1, equations 1-2; pp. 2, 4, 12, 14).

contrasts.reported: Consensus level rises from 0.534 (32B) to 0.725 (7B): z = 14.143, p < 0.001. Higher similarity is coded as lower diversity.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4, final paragraph; p. 14, Figure 3f.

diversity_detail.metric: Consensus strength C(T): average pairwise cosine similarity after the paper's within-player centering and group aggregation; larger values indicate greater similarity.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: all-MiniLM-L6-v2; mean pooling and L2 normalization (PDF p. 7, Methods M1).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each final-round description against all other descriptions in the same session, followed by aggregation over the session. N = 24 counts human and agent players together, not 24 human participants in AI conditions (PDF pp. 7 and 16).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: The paper reports z statistics and p values without identifying the observations, exact test, resampling scheme or dependence correction. Figure 1b’s caption states 95% CI, although its panel displays boxplots; numerical CI limits and their construction are not stated. Figure 3d/f also displays boxplots without defining their observation unit. Independent-session replication and participant- or session-clustered precision are not established (PDF pp. 2, 4, 7, 12, 14).
diversity_detail.notes: Contrast directions reverse similarity to the codebook’s diversity convention. Statistics keep their printed signs. The score pools human and AI descriptions and does not isolate diversity across human writers. No effect size, unprinted mean, standard error, number of independent sessions or analyzed-human count has been derived.

outcomes.name: Conceptual-lexical ratio under agent-capability manipulation (CLR)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Computed from the mixed human-agent output pool. Attribution measures whose expressions enter the consensus, not the number or diversity of ideas and not rated creativity. No uncertainty estimates are printed. CLR = (Ccon + ε)/(Clex + ε), with ε = 0.01; larger values indicate agent influence more concentrated at the conceptual than the lexical level. The smoothing explains nonzero CLR even when Ccon is zero. Robustness to early-diffusion windows of 1–3 rounds is grouped with this outcome. PDF p. 8, Methods M2, equation (4); pp. 17-18, contribution definitions. Study C robustness: Supplementary Figure 6, p. 26. Lexical and conceptual contribution components are retained separately as S3-O3 and S3-O4.

contrasts.reported: CLR decreases by 22.9%, from 0.599 (32B) to 0.462 (7B). No uncertainty estimate is printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF pp. 4-5, model-capability comparison; p. 14, Figure 3g.

outcomes.name: Lexical-level agent contribution under agent-capability manipulation
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Population-normalized agent attribution of the stable vocabulary, not a creativity or diversity rating. Words must appear in every one of the final 5 rounds; early human/agent usage is normalized by population share, and attribution scores are weighted by each word's total usage count across the final 5 rounds. Default early-diffusion window is 3 rounds; windows of 1-3 rounds are robustness variants of this same outcome (p. 7, M2; p. 17, equations S1-S3; p. 26, Supplementary Figure 6). Higher values mean more AI lexical influence, with no automatic interpretation as greater creativity. This is a descriptive contribution score on the mixed human-agent output pool. The source does not designate primary or secondary outcomes.

contrasts.reported: Printed default-window labels (window = 3): 7B 0.51; 32B 0.61. These are rounded labels printed on the figure, not values calculated from CLR. No uncertainty estimate is supplied.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 26, Supplementary Figure 6a, red window = 3 bars; p. 25, Supplementary Figure 4 caption defines the panels.

outcomes.name: Conceptual-level agent contribution under agent-capability manipulation
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Population-normalized agent attribution of stable semantic clusters, not the number of distinct ideas. spaCy scene graphs and soft SPICE similarities are clustered using HDBSCAN with Optuna-selected parameters. Clusters represented in every one of the final 5 rounds are weighted by their total usage counts across those final 5 rounds; early-diffusion attribution parallels lexical attribution. Windows of 1-3 rounds are robustness variants (p. 8, M2; pp. 17-18, Supplementary Agent Contribution; p. 26, Supplementary Figure 6). Higher values mean more AI conceptual influence, not necessarily greater creativity. This is a descriptive contribution score on the mixed human-agent output pool. The source does not designate primary or secondary outcomes.

old.reason: Study A satisfies all three criteria. Human assignment to experimental conditions is explicitly randomized (PDF p. 16, Participants); agent proportions vary and a pure-human comparison condition is present. Prior AI-generated partner descriptions remain visible while later human descriptions are produced (p. 22, Supplementary Figure 1). Supplementary Figure 8a contains 21 human nodes labeled H_0-H_20 at 12.5% agents, 16 labeled H_0-H_15 at 33.3%, 12 labeled H_0-H_11 at 50%, and 6 labeled H_0-H_5 at 75%. These are human participants analyzed in the influence networks, not agents, edges, output counts or repeated rounds. The figure-derived tally is 21 + 16 + 12 + 6 = 55 distinct analyzed humans across four Study A arms; assignment to one condition is explicit on p. 16. This establishes at least 55 analyzed humans in Study A without asserting an exact full-study or consensus-specific analyzed total. PDF pp. 20-21, Influence Network Analysis; p. 28, Supplementary Figure 8a and caption; p. 16, Participants. Consensus is semantic similarity computed on actual written descriptions (p. 2, Results; p. 7, Methods M1, equations 1-2), and the codebook includes writing tasks compared across people for similarity. The 127 recruited people are not used as a single study's analyzed N, and the allocation roster is not treated as a completion count. Mixed human-agent output pools, unknown consensus analysis units and precision, and possible internal comparator reuse limit extraction and pooling; they do not overturn these study-level eligibility criteria.
